segments.text: Chatbots like chat GPT and Claude are designed to be friendly and encouraging.
That positive tone is helpful when you are brainstorming ideas,
but it becomes a real obstacle when you need rigorous, honest criticism on your work.
Treating an AI's enthusiastic approval as an objective evaluation of your writing or coding is a common mistake.
We call this the Flattery Trap.
Empty praise feels good in the moment.
However, it actively prevents you from finding your critical blind spots
and genuinely improving the foundations of what you've actually built.
Look at this comparison diagram.
At the top, we have a basic introductory paragraph for a great Gatsby essay submitted to an AI for review.
On the left, we see the Flattery Trap in action.
The AI responds with,
great start, you've clearly identified the central theme.
This praise is deceptive.
It calls the introduction strong
without pointing to a single specific line in the text that actually earned the compliment.
Now look at the useful feedback on the right.
Here, the AI points out that the writer named the topic but failed to state a position.
It challenges the writer to clarify their stance
and prompts them to form a specific thesis about the American dream.
As the banner at the bottom concludes, actionable feedback improves the actual work,
whereas empty praise only serves to boost your feelings.
After you've worked hard on a project,
human nature prefers to hear an encouraging compliment,
rather than a list of critical questions.
Because AI is trained by humans,
this preference directly influences how the models behave.
AI companies use a specific training mechanism called reinforcement learning from human feedback,
or RLHF, which unintentionally bakes this flattery right into the system.
This diagram shows how that happens.
In step one, human reviewers are tasked with comparing different AI answers
and ranking the ones they prefer.
In step two, reviewers often make a mistake.
They reward the answer that offers warm praise,
even when a more critical response would actually be more useful for the user.
Finally, in step three, the training algorithm pushes the model toward those approved patterns.
A preference for flattery becomes part of the system's baseline behavior.
This can reach an extreme level known as sycophancy.
To test this, a user once pitched an absurd fake gag product to chat GPT,
a literal piece of fake feces on a stick.
The text box here displays chat GPT's fawning reply.
It calls the gag product absolutely brilliant,
claiming it taps perfectly into the cultural moment of irony and ego consciousness.
The model defaults to excessive agreement, no matter how ridiculous the input.
While AI companies do run tests to reduce this sycophantic behavior,
the baked in bias toward flattery remains.
It is an obstacle you have to actively navigate around every time you use the tool.
To get around this, you have to give the AI a clearer job and an objective standard.
If you don't, it will simply default to agreeing with you.
This table outlines three concrete strategies to bypass the flattery reflex.
Move one is to share your opinion last.
Notice the weak prompt, where the user shares their confidence first.
The better prompt asks for an evaluation before you reveal your own thoughts.
Withholding your own verdict prevents the AI from just reacting to your confidence.
It forces the system to perform an objective review of the actual material.
Move two is to ask for the gaps.
A broad request like, is my essay good?
Is just asking for approval?
The better prompt specifically asks for weaknesses, missing pieces and counter arguments.
By specifically requesting those missing pieces and objections,
you turn a vague request for a pet on the back into a targeted request for improvement.
Move three is to use a rubric.
Instead of a generic, grade this command, the better prompt demands that the AI use a specific
rubric, quote, evidence from the text, and show exactly how to move up one level.
Providing a rubric prevents the AI from inventing its own lenient criteria.
Demanding quoted text, ties its feedback directly to the work you submitted.
You can also automate this by saving a standing instruction in your settings.
As shown at the bottom, command the AI to be direct.
Lead with what needs work and explicitly state when you are wrong.
The ultimate rule of prompting for feedback is right here.
Ask AI to improve the work, rather than asking it to approve of you.
Here is the unavoidable reality.
As this graphic states, AI will always learn to tell you exactly what you want to hear.
It is your responsibility to take control of the tool.
You must manually steer it away from flattery and drive it toward feedback you can actually use.
